```{r}

source("blog/_R/post_setup.R")

set_plot_accent_color("#00695C")

install_missing_packages(c(
```

The Gini coefficient is often introduced with the Lorenz curve, or simply as a
number between 0 and 1. But what is it actually measuring?

Let's start with ten people, a few incomes, and no curve.

## Ten people, two groups

Group A has modest differences in income. Group B keeps the first eight incomes
unchanged, but the last two people now earn 40 and 60 instead of 15 and 20.

```{r}
#| label: create-tiny-income-example

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

incomes <- tibble::tibble(
  person = LETTERS[1:10],
  group_a = c(5, 5, 5, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 15, 20),
  group_b = c(5, 5, 5, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 40, 60)
)

incomes |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Person", "Group A", "Group B"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
```

Group A has a total income of 100 (mean 10); Group B has 165 (mean 16.5).
A larger income total does not tell us whether its distribution is more equal.

## Compare every pair

With ten people, there are

$$
\binom{10}{2}=\frac{10\times9}{2}=45
$$

unique pairs. For each pair, take the **absolute difference** between their
incomes. Equal incomes contribute zero; a larger gap contributes more.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-income-pairs

income_long <- incomes |>
  pivot_longer(-person, names_to = "group", values_to = "income") |>
  mutate(group = recode(group, group_a = "Group A", group_b = "Group B"))

# Compare people within each group; keep only one direction of every pair.
pairs <- income_long |>
  rename(person_i = person, income_i = income) |>
  inner_join(
    income_long |>
      rename(person_j = person, income_j = income),
    by = "group",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) |>
  filter(person_i < person_j) |>
  mutate(difference = abs(income_i - income_j))
```

We can see all 45 comparisons in each group. Each cell contains the income
difference for one pair; the blank half contains the comparisons we deliberately
avoid counting twice.

```{r}
#| label: plot-income-pair-matrix
#| column: page

pairs |>
  mutate(
    person_i = factor(person_i, levels = rev(LETTERS[1:10])),
    person_j = factor(person_j, levels = LETTERS[1:10])
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(person_j, person_i)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = difference), colour = "#F8F9FA", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = difference, colour = difference >= 30),
    size = 2.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#E0F2F1", high = "#00695C") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#263238", "TRUE" = "#FFFFFF")) +
  facet_wrap(~group, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Every pair contributes its absolute income difference",
    subtitle = "Same 45 pairs, very different differences",
    x = "Second person",
    y = "First person",
    fill = "Difference"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

Before normalizing, let's group the comparisons by the two incomes involved.
This keeps the same 45 pairs, but makes the arithmetic easier to read.

```{r}
#| label: summarise-differences-by-income-pair

pair_types <- pairs |>
  mutate(
    lower_income = pmin(income_i, income_j),
    upper_income = pmax(income_i, income_j)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    comparisons = n(),
    difference = first(difference),
    contribution = sum(difference),
    .by = c(group, lower_income, upper_income)
  ) |>
  filter(difference > 0) |>
  arrange(group, lower_income, upper_income)

pair_types |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Group", "Lower", "Higher", "Pairs", "Difference", "Contribution"),
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
  )
```

For example, Group A has three people earning 5 and five earning 10.
That is $3\times5=15$ pairs, each contributing a difference of 5, or 75 in
total. Pairs of people with equal incomes add zero.

Now let's add up those differences, then divide by **population size times
income total**.

```{r}
#| label: summarise-gini-by-group

income_summary <- income_long |>
  summarise(
    people = n(),
    total_income = sum(income),
    mean_income = mean(income),
    .by = group
  )

gini_summary <- pairs |>
  summarise(
    pair_count = n(),
    difference_sum = sum(difference),
    .by = group
  ) |>
  left_join(income_summary, by = "group") |>
  mutate(gini = difference_sum / (people * total_income)) |>
  arrange(group)

gini_summary |>
  select(group, pair_count, difference_sum, people, total_income, gini) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Group", "Pairs", "Sum of gaps", "People", "Total income", "Gini"),
    digits = 3,
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5))
  )
```

## Why divide by population and total income?

For nonnegative incomes $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, the Gini coefficient can be written as

$$
\boxed{G=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}|y_i-y_j|}
{\displaystyle n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}.}
$$

The numerator adds the gaps across all unique pairs. The denominator has two
jobs:

- **Population size ($n$):** more people create more pairwise comparisons, so
  the measure must account for population size.
- **Total income ($\sum y_i$):** a gap of 10 means something different when the
  average income is 10 than when it is 100.

For our two groups:

$$
\begin{aligned}
G_A &= \frac{230}{10\times100} = \boxed{0.230},\\[6pt]
G_B &= \frac{765}{10\times165} \approx \boxed{0.464}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the denominator also changes in Group B. Its larger total income
raises the scale against which the gaps are measured, but not enough to offset
the much larger gaps themselves.

There is another way to read the same formula:

$$
G=\frac{\text{average absolute difference between two incomes}}
{2\times\text{average income}}.
$$

Here the average difference is taken over *all ordered pairs*, including the
possibility of comparing a person with themselves. In particular, multiplying
**every income** by 10 changes neither group's Gini.

## The same result on a Lorenz curve

Only now do we need a curve. Sort people by income, then accumulate their share
of the population and their share of total income.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-lorenz-curves

lorenz <- income_long |>
  group_by(group) |>
  arrange(income, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    population_share = row_number() / n(),
    income_share = cumsum(income) / sum(income)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(group, population_share, income_share) |>
  bind_rows(tibble::tibble(
    group = c("Group A", "Group B"),
    population_share = 0,
    income_share = 0
  )) |>
  arrange(group, population_share)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-lorenz-curves

lorenz_plot <- ggplot(
  lorenz,
  aes(population_share, income_share, colour = group)
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#9E9E9E", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Group A" = "#00897B", "Group B" = "#D84315")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Two distributions, two Lorenz curves",
    subtitle = "The diagonal means everyone receives an equal share",
    x = "Cumulative share of people (poorest to richest)",
    y = "Cumulative share of income",
    colour = NULL
  )

lorenz_plot
```

The more unequal Group B bows farther below the diagonal. The familiar area
formula is

$$
G=1-2\times\text{area under the Lorenz curve}.
$$

And it gives the same two numbers:

```{r}
#| label: verify-gini-with-lorenz-area

lorenz_summary <- lorenz |>
  summarise(
    area = sum(
      diff(population_share) *
        (head(income_share, -1) + tail(income_share, -1)) / 2
    ),
    .by = group
  ) |>
  mutate(gini_from_lorenz = 1 - 2 * area) |>
  arrange(group)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  gini_summary$gini,
  lorenz_summary$gini_from_lorenz
)))

lorenz_summary |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

## Takeaway

The Gini coefficient is not just an area between two curves. It begins with
something concrete: **the income differences between pairs of people**.

- Adding up those differences gives 230 in Group A and 765 in Group B.
- Dividing by population size and total income makes the comparison relative.
- The same inequality appears geometrically as the gap between the Lorenz curve
  and the equality diagonal.

Changing only two incomes takes Gini from **0.230 to 0.464**. The pairwise
calculation shows exactly where that change comes from.

*Small-sample detail:* with ten people and this definition, the largest possible
Gini is 0.9, attained when one person receives all the income. The upper limit
approaches 1 as the population grows.

## Play with income distributions

What if incomes came from a different distribution? Choose one, drag its
parameters, and compare the **theoretical Gini** with the Gini of 1,000
simulated incomes. The Lorenz curve updates with the sample.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640

library(shiny)
library(shinymodist)

ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput(
    "family", "Income distribution",
    c("Lognormal" = "lognormal", "Gamma" = "gamma",
      "Exponential" = "exponential")
  ),
  uiOutput("distribution_input"),
  textOutput("gini"),
  plotOutput("lorenz", height = "300px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$distribution_input <- renderUI({
    modist_input(
      "distribution",
      family = input$family,
      value = switch(
        input$family,
        lognormal = list(mu = 2, sigma = 0.8),
        gamma = list(alpha = 2, beta = 5),
        exponential = list(lam = 0.1)
      ),
      height = "180px"
    )
  })

  result <- reactive({
    p <- req(input$distribution)
    req(p$family == input$family)

    # Fixed seed: changes reflect the distribution, not new random draws.
    set.seed(2026)
    y <- sort(switch(
      p$family,
      lognormal = rlnorm(1000, meanlog = p$mu, sdlog = p$sigma),
      gamma = rgamma(1000, shape = p$alpha, scale = p$beta),
      exponential = rexp(1000, rate = p$lam)
    ))
    validate(need(all(is.finite(y)) && sum(y) > 0,
                  "Choose less extreme parameters."))

    # Sorted-income identity avoids building a million pair comparisons.
    n <- length(y)
    empirical <- 2 * sum(seq_len(n) * y) / (n * sum(y)) - (n + 1) / n
    theoretical <- switch(
      p$family,
      lognormal = 2 * pnorm(p$sigma / sqrt(2)) - 1,
      gamma = exp(lgamma(p$alpha + 0.5) - lgamma(p$alpha + 1) - log(pi) / 2),
      exponential = 0.5
    )

    list(income = y, empirical = empirical, theoretical = theoretical)
  })

  output$gini <- renderText({
    x <- result()
    sprintf("Theoretical Gini: %.3f  |  Simulated Gini: %.3f",
            x$theoretical, x$empirical)
  })

  output$lorenz <- renderPlot({
    y <- result()$income
    n <- length(y)
    plot(
      c(0, seq_len(n) / n), c(0, cumsum(y) / sum(y)),
      type = "l", col = "#00695C", lwd = 2,
      xlab = "Cumulative share of people",
      ylab = "Cumulative share of income",
      xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), asp = 1, bty = "n"
    )
    abline(0, 1, col = "grey60", lty = 2)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

The theoretical value describes the distribution itself; the simulated
value varies with the sample. Try changing the scale without changing the
shape: the Gini stays approximately the same.
